pl-l2d23c1-d1e108.summary: Asks why God permitted man to be tempted when he foreknew he would be deceived.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e111.summary: Answers with Augustine: it would not be praiseworthy for man to live well only because no one urged him to live badly, since he had the power by nature, with God's help, not to consent; and not consenting is more glorious than being unable to be tempted.
claims: Resisting temptation is more glorious than being untemptable.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e114.summary: Answers why God created those he foresaw would be evil: he foresaw what good he would make of their evils; he left them the ability to act so that, acting culpably, they would find him acting laudably. Evil will is from themselves; good nature and just punishment from him; he knew they would profit the good and be justly punished.
claims: God foresaw the good he would draw from evil.
Evil will is from the creature; nature and punishment from God.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e118.summary: Reports the objection: God should have made man such that he would not will to sin at all.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e126.summary: Grants that a nature wholly unwilling to sin is better, but insists one made able not to sin if it willed is not evil and is justly punished when it sins voluntarily; God made both to be praised the more, the former in the holy angels, the latter in men.
claims: A nature able not to sin is good.
God made both kinds of nature.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e132.summary: Reports the objection: if God willed, they too would be good.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e135.summary: Grants this, but says God willed rather that they be what they willed, the good not fruitlessly and the evil not unpunished.
claims: God willed creatures to be what they chose.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e138.summary: Reports the objection: God, being omnipotent, could turn their wills to good.

pl-l2d23c1-d1e144.summary: Answers: he could; why did he not? Because he would not. Why would he not? He knows. We should not be wiser than we ought.
claims: God could have converted them but did not will to.
The reason is hidden in God.

pl-l2d23c1.summary: Asks why God permitted man to be tempted when he foreknew he would be deceived. It would not be praiseworthy to live well only because no one urged evil; man had the power, with God's help, not to consent, and not consenting is more glorious than being unable to be tempted. Why did God create those he foreknew would be evil? Because he foresaw the good he would make of their evils: they have their evil will from themselves, from him a good nature and just punishment. A nature unwilling to sin would be better, but one able not to sin if it willed is not evil, and God made both, angels and men. God could have made them good or turned their wills, but willed otherwise; why, he knows, and we should not be wiser than we ought.
claims: God permitted temptation because resisting it is praiseworthy and more glorious than being untemptable.
Man could, with God's help, refuse consent.
God created those he foreknew would be evil because he foresaw the good he would draw from them.
Evil will is from the creature; good nature and just punishment are from God.
A nature able not to sin is good, though one unable to will sin is better.
Why God did not turn their wills is known to him alone.
